appendix.title: Pitfalls
appendix.para: The bridge's rules are few, and each follows from a difference between the two languages. These are the places where they surprise.

listitem.para: Without arguments, a function or a method is called, not returned: server~handle_request runs it. To pass a method as a value (a callback, a thread's target), take it with o~getattr("handle_request").

varlistentry.term: Names in any case can pick the wrong attribute

listitem.para: Of logging.info and logging.INFO, the lowercase one wins, so logging~INFO calls the function (and fails, as it wants a message). The constant is logging~getattr("INFO").

varlistentry.term: Text that looks like a number becomes a number

listitem.para: "2026" goes as the int 2026, which os.path.join("dir", "2026") refuses, and d["1"] is d[1]. Use .py~str("2026"), or import the module as "string" ().
o[0] is the first item of a Python list or tuple, and server_address[1] the port. counts from 1.
class, isA, string, hasMethod and the other methods of Rexx's Object are Rexx's: l~class is PyObject, Python's is l~getattr("__class__"). copy, send, start, run and request are the exception ().
.py~dict is the class dict, not an empty dict: classes are returned, so that their attributes can be reached. Make an instance with .py~dict~new.

varlistentry.term: Python's str, int and float on &py; are the bridge's

listitem.para: .py~str(x) keeps the result as a PyObject, and .py~str without an argument is an empty one, not the class: to name the class, as a base or a type, write "str" (.py~extend(self, "str")) or .py~getattr("str").

varlistentry.term: Operators need the Python object on the left

listitem.para: Python's bytes come to Rexx as Rexx strings, and a Rexx string goes as a str (or a number): to write to a binary stream, .py~box("bytes", text).
